questions.stem: Two employees perform the same work at the same air temperature, but one works in much higher humidity. Why is the high-humidity worker generally at greater risk of heat strain?
options: High humidity reduces sweat evaporation, limiting a major pathway for the body to release heat.
High humidity causes all sweat to evaporate immediately and overcools the body.
Humidity affects only equipment corrosion and has no influence on human heat exchange.
The risk increases only because humid air contains less oxygen than dry air at the same conditions.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Sweat cools effectively when it evaporates. When the surrounding air already contains substantial moisture, evaporation slows even if sweating increases, so internal heat can accumulate.
incorrectOptionExplanations: High humidity reduces, rather than accelerates, evaporative capacity.
Humidity is a major environmental determinant of evaporative cooling.
The central heat-stress mechanism in this comparison is impaired evaporation, not a meaningful oxygen reduction.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 4 - Heat Stress
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 13, human heat balance and heat stress, pp. 367-371; OSHA OTM Section III, Chapter 4, environmental heat and evaporation

questions.stem: A worker in a hot area becomes confused, speaks unclearly, stumbles, and has a very high body temperature. The worker is still sweating. What is the best interpretation?
options: Exclude heat stroke because the worker is still sweating, then treat the condition as uncomplicated heat exhaustion with oral fluids and routine observation.
Suspect heat stroke and treat the altered mental status as a medical emergency even though sweating is present.
The findings indicate only heat rash because the symptoms involve the skin and heat.
The worker should finish the task slowly and be evaluated after the shift.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Confusion, slurred speech, loss of coordination, seizures, or unconsciousness are critical heat-stroke signs. Sweating may be absent or profuse, so its presence does not rule out heat stroke.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Current guidance recognizes that exertional heat stroke may occur with heavy sweating.
Heat rash does not explain severe neurologic changes and very high temperature.
Delay can lead to death or permanent disability; emergency response and rapid cooling are required.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 4 - Heat Stress; CDC/NIOSH - First Aid for Heat Illness
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 13, heat stroke, pp. 370-371; OSHA heat-stress illness recognition; NIOSH heat-illness first aid

questions.stem: A coworker collapses during heavy outdoor work and shows confusion and seizure activity. What should the crew do first?
options: Give salt tablets and wait thirty minutes before deciding whether medical help is needed.
Place the worker alone in an air-conditioned vehicle, offer water after the seizure stops, and delay emergency assistance unless symptoms persist for at least thirty minutes.
Call emergency medical services immediately, move the worker to a cooler area, begin rapid active cooling, and keep someone with the worker.
Offer a large amount of water by mouth while the worker is seizing.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Suspected heat stroke is time critical. Emergency care and rapid cooling should begin at once; the worker should not be left alone or expected to recover by resting without observation.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Salt tablets are not emergency treatment, and delaying care is dangerous.
The worker can deteriorate quickly and requires continuous observation, cooling, and emergency care.
Oral fluids can create an aspiration hazard in a person with altered consciousness or seizures.
questions.sourceTitle: OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 4 - Heat Stress; CDC/NIOSH - First Aid for Heat Illness
questions.sourceLocation: OSHA heat-stress medical-emergency guidance; NIOSH first aid for exertional heat stroke

questions.stem: A new employee will begin a full-duration job in a hot environment. Which initial schedule best follows current NIOSH acclimatization guidance?
options: Assign 100% of the normal hot-work duration on day 1 so acclimatization occurs faster.
Keep the employee in the hot area without work for one hour, then assign the full workload.
Use the same full-duration schedule as a fully acclimatized worker, but add one extra water break because age, experience, and recent heat exposure do not change acclimatization needs.
Limit day 1 to no more than 20% of the usual heat exposure and increase by no more than 20% on each additional day, with close supervision.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: New workers need gradual exposure over approximately 7 to 14 days. The 20% progression reduces early-shift risk while physiological adaptations develop.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Full exposure on the first day substantially increases heat-illness risk and does not safely accelerate adaptation.
Acclimatization is specific to the heat and work demand and develops over repeated days, not a brief passive exposure.
New or returning workers require a deliberate progression and close monitoring.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); CDC/NIOSH - Heat Stress Acclimatization
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 13, acclimatization, p. 372; NIOSH acclimatization schedule for new workers

questions.stem: During moderate work in heat lasting less than two hours, which hydration instruction is most consistent with NIOSH guidance for a typical worker without a medical fluid restriction?
options: Drink about 1 cup (8 oz.) of water at intervals of 15 to 20 minutes rather than relying on thirst alone.
Drink nothing during the task and replace the entire loss after the shift.
Take salt tablets with each cup of water and avoid ordinary meals during the shift, regardless of work duration, diet, or medical conditions.
Drink more than 2 quarts every hour to ensure that dehydration is impossible.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Frequent small amounts help replace sweat losses before thirst becomes a reliable warning. Needs vary with conditions and individual factors, and excessive fluid intake should also be avoided.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Delayed replacement permits dehydration and performance decline during exposure.
NIOSH does not recommend routine salt tablets; regular meals usually replace electrolytes.
Excessive intake can cause dangerous low blood sodium; fluid intake must remain reasonable.
questions.sourceTitle: CDC/NIOSH - Workplace Recommendations for Heat Stress
questions.sourceLocation: NIOSH workplace heat recommendations, hydration for moderate activity and limits on excessive intake

questions.stem: At an outdoor work area with direct solar load, the natural wet-bulb temperature is 83 deg F, globe temperature is 104 deg F, and dry-bulb temperature is 94 deg F. What is the WBGT?
options: 83.7 deg F
88.3 deg F
93.7 deg F
98.5 deg F
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Outdoor WBGT = 0.7(83) + 0.2(104) + 0.1(94) = 58.1 + 20.8 + 9.4 = 88.3 deg F. The result must then be interpreted with workload, clothing, acclimatization, and work-rest criteria.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This result underweights radiant and dry-bulb contributions and does not follow the outdoor WBGT equation.
This value is close to an unweighted average and does not apply the 70/20/10 factors.
This result overweights the globe and dry-bulb temperatures.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 4 - Heat Stress
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 13, outdoor WBGT equation, pp. 374-375; OSHA OTM Section III, Chapter 4, outdoor WBGT calculation

questions.stem: Inside a building with no solar load, the natural wet-bulb temperature is 78 deg F and globe temperature is 90 deg F. What is the WBGT?
options: 78.0 deg F
84.0 deg F
81.6 deg F
86.4 deg F
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Indoor or no-solar-load WBGT = 0.7(78) + 0.3(90) = 54.6 + 27.0 = 81.6 deg F.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This uses only the wet-bulb reading and omits radiant heat represented by the globe temperature.
This is a simple average of the two measurements rather than the required weighted equation.
This reverses or misapplies the 70% wet-bulb and 30% globe weights.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 4 - Heat Stress
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 13, indoor/no-solar WBGT equation, pp. 374-375; OSHA OTM Section III, Chapter 4

questions.stem: A worker performs heavy whole-body work at 7.0 kcal/min for 60 min, sits at 0.3 kcal/min for 30 min, and performs light whole-body work at 3.5 kcal/min for 90 min. What is the time-weighted average metabolic rate?
options: Approximately 3.60 kcal/min, or 216 kcal/h
Approximately 5.28 kcal/min, or 317 kcal/h
Approximately 7.00 kcal/min, or 420 kcal/h
4.13 kcal/min, or about 248 kcal/h
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Average = [(7.0x60) + (0.3x30) + (3.5x90)] / 180 = 744 / 180 = 4.13 kcal/min. Multiplying by 60 gives about 248 kcal/h.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This is close to an unweighted average and ignores the different task durations.
This overweights the heavy-work period relative to the total 180 minutes.
This uses only the highest task rate and ignores the rest and lighter-work periods.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 13, time-weighted average metabolic rate and workload categories, pp. 372-374

questions.stem: A crew changes from light clothing to vapor-barrier protective suits while performing the same heavy task in the same weather. What should the heat-stress assessment do?
options: Account for the added clothing and metabolic burden and consider shorter work periods, longer cooling rest, and other controls rather than using the previous schedule unchanged.
Keep the previous work-rest schedule because ambient temperature and job title are the only variables needed for heat-stress evaluation, even when clothing changes evaporation and metabolic cost.
Increase the work period because the suit prevents hot air from contacting the skin.
Remove hydration and rest breaks so employees finish before the hottest part of the shift.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Impermeable or insulating PPE limits evaporation and adds work burden. Work-rest decisions must account for environmental heat, workload, clothing, acclimatization, and the temperature of the recovery area.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Ambient temperature alone does not represent humidity, radiant heat, workload, or clothing effects.
The suit may trap metabolic heat and moisture and increase heat strain.
Removing recovery controls increases heat-illness risk during heavy work in encapsulating PPE.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 4 - Heat Stress; CDC/NIOSH - Workplace Recommendations for Heat Stress
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 13, work-rest cycles and protective clothing, pp. 372-376; OSHA/NIOSH heat-risk assessment and work-schedule controls

questions.stem: Workers are exposed primarily to intense radiant heat from a furnace face. Which engineering control most directly interrupts that exposure pathway?
options: Increase air humidity so sweat remains on the skin longer.
Install an appropriately designed reflective heat shield between the furnace and the workers while maintaining necessary airflow and visibility.
Issue darker, heavier clothing and reduce air movement around the workers without evaluating evaporation, radiant load, or the added metabolic burden of the garments.
Turn off local process ventilation so warm air remains stationary.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A reflective barrier placed between the source and workers can reduce radiant heat transfer. Other controls may still be needed for convective heat, metabolic load, and process access.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Higher humidity reduces evaporation and may worsen heat strain.
Additional insulation can increase heat strain unless it is specifically designed and evaluated for the radiant hazard.
Removing ventilation can increase heat and contaminant exposure and does not interrupt radiation.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA Technical Manual, Section III, Chapter 4 - Heat Stress
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 13, engineering controls and heat shields, pp. 371-372; OSHA OTM heat-stress engineering controls

questions.stem: A soaked outdoor worker in 45 deg F weather becomes confused, loses coordination, and speaks slowly. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Rule out hypothermia because the air temperature is above 32 deg F, keep the worker outdoors, and monitor for improvement without changing the wet clothing.
Rub the arms and legs vigorously, have the worker exercise hard, and apply direct high heat to the extremities before seeking medical help because movement restores circulation fastest.
Treat the condition as possible hypothermia: obtain medical help, move the worker to a warm dry place, remove wet clothing, insulate the body, and handle the worker gently.
Leave the wet clothing in place, wrap the worker over it, and have the person walk around to generate heat before seeking medical care.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Hypothermia can occur above freezing when rain, sweat, or immersion accelerates heat loss. Confusion and coordination loss are serious signs requiring prompt rewarming and medical evaluation.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Wetness and wind can cause dangerous cooling at temperatures above freezing.
Rough handling and strenuous exercise may be unsafe in moderate or severe hypothermia.
Wet clothing increases heat loss, and exertion or delayed medical evaluation can worsen moderate or severe hypothermia.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); OSHA - Cold Stress Guide
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 13, hypothermia and cold-stress treatment, pp. 380-383; OSHA cold-stress guide

questions.stem: The air temperature is 15 deg F and wind speed is 20 mph. Using the National Weather Service wind-chill equation, what is the approximate wind-chill temperature?
options: 7 deg F
15 deg F
-15 deg F
-2 deg F
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Wind chill = 35.74 + 0.6215(15) - 35.75(20^0.16) + 0.4275(15)(20^0.16) = approximately -2.3 deg F, which rounds to -2 deg F.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This underestimates the additional heat loss caused by a 20-mph wind.
This repeats the air temperature and ignores the wind term.
This overstates the wind effect for the stated temperature and speed.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025); National Weather Service - Understanding Wind Chill
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 13, wind-chill equation and chart, pp. 381-382; National Weather Service wind-chill formula
questions.units: deg F, T in deg F, V in mph
